### 183. ✅ Ch. 11 — Redline 15: charity “the form of the virtues” (line 128); command as self-gift (line 136) (2026-10-09)

Redline 15 (`chapters/reports/ch11-redline15-2026-10-09.html`). Followed Patrick’s question whether Aquinas’s ten questions on prudence (II-II qq.47–56) show a better framework than, or a flaw in, the definition. Finding: no conflict; Aquinas’s foundation is charity ordered to God (q.23 a.7–8, “form of the virtues”), the same ground as the definition; his treatise is the fuller account of *how* prudence works, and the definition is the test of *what* it must protect. The book’s use of truth, justice, mercy and sacrifice in the three acts is our own wording, compatible with Aquinas, never presented as his scheme. Patrick: sacrifice and self-gift are interchangeable anywhere; line 132 (justice in deliberation) stands, since the justice chapter covers the sense of justice God places in us. The Shape of a Wise Decision: line 128 adds “That is no accident. As we saw in Chapter 5, on how love binds every virtue together, the Church calls charity ‘the form of the virtues’ (*CCC* 1827). Prudence is not a second rule standing beside love; it is love doing its thinking.” (CCC 1827 is Chapter 5’s opening quote.) Line 136: “the acting will cost something. That cost is sacrifice” → “in acting it gives itself. That self-gift is sacrifice”. Pre-edit copy: `archive/ch11-pre-2026-10-06/chapter_11.pre-r15.md`. Verified: file identical to the dry run (re-staged, cmp).

### 163. ✅ Ch. 10 — Redline 33: family examples for the four “unity without” paragraphs; father and mother (2026-10-06)

Redline 33 (`chapters/reports/ch10-redline33-2026-10-06.html`), lines 294–300, eight edits. Each paragraph now leads with everyday family examples, both for the pillar missing and for the pillar pushed alone.

Truth: a couple who stopped telling each other the truth replaces the propaganda nation; truth alone is the parent who is always right and never kind, then the parish whose orthodoxy drives wounded people out. Justice: the mother taken for granted, the sibling caring for an aging parent alone, the overlooked child, the marriage; justice alone is the controlling, over-critical father. Mercy: brothers estranged since the funeral, the daughter punished for a mistake at sixteen; mercy alone is the mother who pays the grown son’s debts and covers for him. Sacrifice: parents who give everything except time; sacrifice alone is the mother who gives while no one gives back.

New paragraph: the father who leans toward justice and the mother who leans toward mercy, grounded in CCC 2333 (complementarity), ending with God the Father, in whom justice and mercy are one. Patrick asked for family examples and the father/mother point. Honest limit recorded: the Church teaches complementarity but does not map justice to fathers and mercy to mothers, hence “leans” and “part of how God made us.” Cartel, insiders and propaganda removed. Cache: ccc/2333.json (canonical). Verified: file identical to the dry run; footnotes unchanged; divs 9/9.

### 151. ✅ Ch. 10 — Redline 19: Ignatius in history — Polycarp and the Roman Canon (2026-10-03)

Redline 19 (`chapters/reports/ch10-redline19-2026-10-03.html`). After the Ignatius quotation (line 217): “We know him from more than his own letters. His friend St. Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, gathered those letters and sent them on to the church at Philippi, holding up ‘the blessed Ignatius’ as an example of patience.\<sup\>2\</sup\> And the Church still names him among the martyrs in the Roman Canon, the oldest Eucharistic Prayer of the Roman Rite.” Note 2: Polycarp, *Letter to the Philippians* 9, 13, ANF 1. Patrick asked to attest Ignatius's historical concreteness. Answered first: Ignatius was never formally canonized (the process did not exist; first papal canonization 993); recognized from the beginning by the Church's worship (feast 17 October; Roman Canon). In the current Missal his name in the Nobis quoque list is optional, so the text says the Church “names him,” not every Mass. Cache: other/polycarp-philippians.json; Missal Nobis quoque list. Verified: file identical to the dry run; \<sup\> 1–2 match Notes 1–2; divs 9/9.

### 54. ✅ Ch. 6 — one deposit: Sacred Tradition named, Scripture within it (2026-09-24)

Answer given: not in those words — she keeps them distinct (CCC 78, 81) — but they come from one source and “form one thing” (CCC 80); the Bible was born within Tradition (DV 7), its canon is known through Tradition (CCC 120; DV 8), and it is read within Tradition (CCC 113). Correction offered on his reasoning: Scripture is named separately chiefly because it alone is inspired, “the speech of God … put down in writing under the breath of the Holy Spirit” (CCC 81), not mainly as the best historical record; the Gospels are “the heart of all the Scriptures” (CCC 125). Patrick's key point, adopted: they are not two deposits but one.

Applied after one rejected draft (CCC 80 appended at the end read as “an afterthought”): the paragraph now runs — the Church's life in those centuries → “the Church calls this living transmission Sacred Tradition” → “the Scriptures were never a second deposit standing beside it” (written within it, recognized by it, CCC 120, read within it) → “Scripture is the Word of God set down in writing, Tradition is the same Word handed on in the Church's life, and the Church insists they are one” + CCC 80 → “That is why …” CCC 82 (both sentences). CCC 80 and 82 quoted from the USCCB edition. 11,506 → 11,620 words. Verified: file identical to the dry run; structure and `<sup>`1–7 intact. Review doc still to rebuild (last built at entry 50).

**Same day:** the “Consider what those three centuries held” paragraph split into three at Patrick's request (“too long”), no words changed — Scripture read inside the Church's life / the Church's spread by the time the canon was settled / Sacred Tradition, one deposit. ### 47. ✅ Ch. 6 — “The Fundamental Truths of Human Existence” rebuilt as five truths (2026-09-20/24)

At Patrick's request, after entry 46. Plan approved first, then redlined and revised over several rounds; group 1 written 2026-09-24, groups 2–4 the same day. 9,902 → 10,552 words. Redline at `chapters/reports/ch06-redline2-2026-09-20.html`; review doc rebuilt at `chapters/reports/ch06-review-2026-09-24.html`, same key `wil-ch06-suggestions-v1`.

**The shape.** The three bold truths became five, each a feature of the image of God that the closing Genesis 1:27 paragraph names: (1) *We exist, and we did not have to* — ends “Our very existence is a gift, given before we could ask for it”; (2) *We are alive, and the rock is not* — Patrick's rock: the same elements as the soil and stones, “A rock cannot bring a rock to life, or know what it is for,” Genesis 2:7 whole, CCC 366, “None of us is an accident”; (3) *We are someone, not something* — intellect and will, CCC 356–357, and the hinge to “God Has Made Truth Accessible”; (4) man or woman, two paragraphs; (5) made for love, with CCC 357. The close maps each truth to God: He is / we receive being; He lives / we live; He knows and wills / we know and choose; He is a communion of Persons / we are man and woman, for one another and for love.

**Truth 4, Patrick's points.** Sex is “not one more trait on a list with race, height and birthplace. It is the first distinction within humanity itself” (his “first sub-category under human”). Given by the Creator “body and soul together as one person, and so it is ours to receive, not to rewrite.” Equal dignity (CCC 369, 2335), and the second paragraph opens “Yet men and women are not interchangeable” — CCC 2335, 2333, “above all in fatherhood and motherhood,” CCC 372. It closes on CCC 365 (the soul is the “form” of the body; “not two natures united”) so that being a man or a woman “is part of who you are,” and sends the reader to CCC 369–373, 2331–2336 and *Mulieris Dignitatem* — the question Patrick wanted the reader to leave with. Line 178's “sameness of *nature* or role” became “sameness in every respect, or sameness of role,” since truth 4 says man and woman share one nature.

✗ **Declined, with reasons that should survive.** (1) “Supernatural” for life: in Church usage it names grace; a bishop reads it that way. Patrick's meaning (purposely created, no accident) is carried by CCC 366. (2) “Miracle”: kept as “a wonder as astonishing as any miracle.” (3) “Body, mind and soul”: the Church's anthropology is body and soul, the mind a power of the soul — Patrick agreed. (4) Rocks cannot “establish any order”: crystals do; left out. (5) Sex as “the greatest differentiator” as a measured fact: replaced by grounds that hold. **Cut at Patrick's direction:** “No natural cause accounts for that” and Benedict XVI's “Each of us is the result of a thought of God” (2005 inaugural homily) — “raises too many objections.” Do not reintroduce either. Also cut: “Before we are anything else, we are received” (not intuitive).

**Hand-off.** Ch. 6 now states the rock/alive fact. Ch. 10 (todo 39) makes the creation-as-love argument and todo 40 the gratitude argument by building on it, not restating it.

Eight Codex rows, none previously triaged, plus the carried-forward line 279 (todo 43). Worked by the entry 42 method: straight to a redline, no triage document. His tie to St. John is marked as tradition, and “A.D. 107” became “early in the second century.”

**Patrick's additions to that row.** (1) A paragraph on what the Church was doing before the canon was settled: Justin's Sunday via CCC 1345; about one in ten of the empire Christian by 300 (Stark / Ehrman / general estimate); three British bishops at Arles 314; more than 250 bishops at Nicaea from three continents and Persia (Eusebius's figure, not the traditional 318); Armenia, Georgia and Ethiopia by the mid-fourth century (Armenia's exact year disputed, left out); the Creed completed 381. ### 42. ✅ Ch. 5 — triaged and revised; John 8 replaced by Rebibbia (2026-09-18/19)

Seven Codex rows, none previously triaged. Fifteen edits across six groups, 4,407 → 5,307 words. The centrepiece section was replaced outright at Patrick's direction.

⚠ **Standing preference, stated this session:** on editing work, do not present verdicts or options for Patrick to rule on first — go straight to the redline with the best improvements, and he approves from there. The Ch. 5 triage document was the last one of its kind.

**John 8 was replaced, not corrected, and the reason should survive.** The first draft corrected the reading (the man is absent though Leviticus 20:10 requires both to die; “let him who is without sin be the first to throw a stone” invokes Deuteronomy 17:7, the witnesses throw first). Patrick then asked whether that made the Mosaic penalty wrong — it does not: the judicial precepts were Israel's civil code and lapsed with its purpose (Aquinas, ST I-II q.104 a.3, “dead indeed, because they have no binding force”; CCC 1963, 1967), and the Law's own procedure already had mercy bound into it. Having worked that through, he judged the passage too fraught for this chapter: defending it costs a page of Mosaic law before the reader gets back to the point, and John 8 is the most weaponized passage in Scripture. **Do not reintroduce it to Ch. 5.** The correct reading already lives, briefly, at `chapter_09.md:217` (“in the conspicuously absent man, missing justice”).

**The replacement: “A Cell in Rebibbia: Perfect Integration.”** Chosen from a field of about twenty, top five offered (John Paul II and Ağca; Peter at the charcoal fire, John 21; Joseph and his brothers, Gen 45/50; Zacchaeus; Confession as a coda). Chosen because justice stays intact without explanation — Ağca went back to his cell — and because a human exemplar bridges from Calvary at line 75 to “how do we practice this” at 139. Set aside with reasons: Nathan and David (adultery, and the child's death), Philemon (slavery), Maria Goretti (sexual violence, contested framing), the Nickel Mines Amish (no justice thread), the Prodigal Son (the father's justice is arguable).

**Every fact verified before drafting:** 13 May 1981, St. Peter's Square, two bullets struck; 17 May, first *Regina Coeli* from the Gemelli, “I pray for the brother who struck me, whom I have sincerely forgiven”; 23 July 1981 life sentence; 27 December 1983, twenty-one minutes alone in the Rebibbia cell, “This is a secret that must remain between him and me,” and to his aides “I have spoken to him as a brother whom I have pardoned and who enjoys my trust,” Ağca knelt and kissed his hand; June 2000 pardoned by Ciampi and deported to Turkey for the 1979 murder of Abdi İpekçi; 27 December 2014, Ağca laid white flowers on the tomb — thirty-one years to the day after the *visit*, not the shooting. Deliberately kept off the page: injury specifics beyond “two bullets” and “hours of surgery,” and the “motherly hand,” which reaches us through Cardinal Sodano rather than in the Pope's own words.

⚠ **Four of Patrick's corrections to the section, each a principle worth keeping.** (1) *Name the saint at the head of a paragraph* — in this book a capital *He* means God, so “He refused the choice” read as Christ. (2) *Credit the binding to Christ, not the man.* “He bound them” became “The love of Christ, which he knew deeply and personally, bound them in him,” and its twin later in the section, “Instead he bound them,” became “Instead, Christ's love bound them.” He did the acts; grace did the binding. (3) *“Fragments” beside a shooting reads as bullet fragments.* “There the fragments begin to pull” became “here the threads begin to pull apart,” and “each fragment alone” became “each thread alone” — *threads* is already the chapter's word for the four. (4) *Justice was also for the offender.* The draft treated the sentence as protection for the public only. Patrick's point, now the paragraph “Look at who was served”: a man who has done something grave knows it; a just punishment can be a mercy to him, and if not a mercy, a teacher of truth — CCC 2266, punishment “has a medicinal scope” and “takes on the value of expiation” when accepted. It closes on his own line, lightly edited: “there is truth, justice and mercy enough to go around to everyone in the room, because someone was willing to bear the cost of all three. That is the power of love—and its own witness that it is real.” (*Validation* became *witness*, the book's established word, per Ch. 3/4's “a witness, not a proof.”)

⚠ **A factual error of mine, caught before it reached the page.** An early draft said he was shot on “the feast of Our Lady of Fatima.” In 1981 it was not yet on the universal calendar — John Paul II himself added the memorial in 2002. The text says “the anniversary of Our Lady's first appearance at Fatima.”

**The other five groups.** *Pastoral (57, 61, 63, 151)*, done first because Ch. 4 line 177 now tells a woman in danger she may leave, and Ch. 5 had handed her the bill: the chapter's own examples are all about *warring*, not leaving, “every future relationship” became “the relationships that follow,” and 151 gained a clause on wounds that need a counselor as well as a catechist. *Counterfeits (21, 23)*: the virtues do not become vices; “counterfeits move in to take their names.” *Judgment (79)*: “you're going to hell” replaced by an example that is genuinely accurate, with “the Church, which has named thousands of saints, has never named a single person damned.” *Sacraments (121, 129)*: the Bread *makes* the Body rather than being identical with it; CCC 1855's venial/mortal distinction, which is this chapter's own frayed-versus-severed metaphor. *Aquinas (71, 73)*: *alicui* carries no notion of cost; the argument stands without claiming the Latin said it. *Atonement (17)*: Ch. 9's own fence, plus CCC 616, love “to the end.” Codex's *bonum* half and most of its sacraments list were downgraded — already labelled as the author's reading, or belonging to a sacraments chapter.

**A cross-reference finally made true.** `chapter_11.md:103` reads: “remember what we saw in Chapter 5: the four facets never actually conflict … mistaking a counterfeit for the real thing.” Before this revision Ch. 5 did not say that — it said truth *becomes* cruelty. The line 23 edit makes Ch. 5 say what Ch. 11 already said it said.

**Process.** The word count was estimated twice in drafts and wrong both times (by ~200). Every edit is now dry-run against a scratch copy before approval — which confirms each anchor matches exactly once and produces the real figure. Also: the `build_review.py` unescape workaround was corrupting literal `<sup>` inside `<code>` spans; it now skips code spans.

**Follow-up, 2026-09-19 — the opening paragraphs (17, 21, 23).** At Patrick's request: line 17 now glosses the term — “the Lord's Passion—the suffering and death He freely accepted for us, from Gethsemane to the Cross” (*freely accepted* keeps “in a single act” true across the span). Lines 21 and 23 were rebuilt to mirror each other, one parent-and-child example per thread in canonical order, each matched by its named counterfeit: the father who is never wrong / cruelty calls itself truth; punishments that settle scores / vengeance calls itself justice; paying for the addiction / enabling calls itself mercy; the parent who gives up everything and keeps the receipt / manipulation calls itself sacrifice. *Sacrifice without justice* is the pairing `chapter_09.md:369` uses (“the martyr parent”), so the chapters agree. Dropped, deliberately: “Mercy without justice becomes the abuser forgiven while victims suffer” — it did not fit a parent-and-child list, and the point is carried at line 81 (“allowing evil to continue and victims to suffer”) and at length in Ch. 4. 5,307 → 5,303 words.

**Second follow-up, same morning — for the parent reading.** Patrick: parents who failed in these ways will read lines 21 and 23, and should see clearly how it failed when they missed the binding — “not as accusation, but as teaching in clarity.” Applied: “settle scores” → his “disciplines without teaching”; “keeps the receipt” (a jab) → “until the gift turns into a debt the child can never repay” (Ch. 9:369's own account); a closing sentence, “In every one of these, the parent was reaching for something good, and missed one thread.” The counterfeit list at 23 now names what the counterfeit looks like rather than a vice: harshness, retribution, enabling (all three from line 81), and “a gift with strings attached.” **Principle for any example a reader may recognize themselves in: show the good they reached for and the thread that went missing; never charge a motive.** 5,303 → 5,327 words.

✗ **Third follow-up — the paragraph added after line 63 was cut at Patrick's direction.** It had said “What deforms a child is the warring, not the leaving,” which contradicts Ch. 4 line 47 (“no child has ever been taught to stop grieving one”) — a wounding/deforming distinction too fine for a reader to hold. Its anti-determinism work was already done by the approved edits at 57 (“like this … can deform”), 61 (“can carry … the relationships that follow”) and 161 (“not permanent”, plus the counselor clause); its safety point belongs to Ch. 4:177; and its opening (“Two things belong here, because a reader may be living inside one of them”) was the book talking about itself. **Do not reintroduce a “warring, not the leaving” claim anywhere — it undercuts Ch. 4's witness of the child.** The section again closes as Patrick wrote it and runs straight into “What Aquinas Already Saw.” 5,327 → 5,228 words.

**Fourth follow-up — naming him with reverence.** Patrick: “the Pope had already spoken” is not a respectful way to refer to our beloved Pope John Paul II. Book convention is “St. John Paul II” (20 uses) or “Pope Saint John Paul II”; the Rebibbia section had fallen short three times. Now: “from his hospital bed, the Holy Father had already given his answer” (the first use of “Holy Father” in the book — apt for 1981, and it avoids naming him in full twice in three sentences); “St. John Paul II was served by a truth…”; “laid white flowers on the tomb of St. John Paul II” (canonized April 2014, before the December visit). Kept: “opened fire on Pope John Paul II” — 1981, before canonization. **Rule: never a bare “the Pope” or “John Paul II” for him.** 5,228 → 5,235 words.

⚠ **Fifth follow-up — the Rebibbia section fact-checked, at Patrick's request, and four of my own claims corrected.** (1) “*Alone* with Ağca in his cell” — false: *Time* lists his secretary, two security agents, a Vatican photographer and a TV crew; the two men sat “close together … in a corner of the cell, out of earshot.” (2) “He did not ask for the sentence to be lifted” — false and the most serious: at the June 2000 pardon, Vatican spokesman Navarro-Valls said John Paul II “had communicated to the Italian authorities that he was favorable to an act of clemency” and “this wish was renewed recently” (Religion News Service). The text now says the sentence stood nineteen years, then Italy pardoned him in the Jubilee Year *with the Pope's own support*, and he was extradited to Turkey to serve the sentence he had escaped for the 1979 murder of Abdi İpekçi — justice and mercy bound across two decades, which strengthens the thesis. ### 41. ✅ Ch. 4 — triaged and revised (2026-09-18)

All seven Codex rows triaged against the chapter text, read in full first, before anything was proposed. Four upheld (three of them narrowed), one half-downgraded, one downgraded to a single word. Fifteen replacements applied after two rounds of redline and approval; 5,439 → 5,966 words.

**The safety row was done first, and on its own.** The chapter said “I'm yours, no matter what” (38), “I'm yours. Period.” (65) and “Notice what's missing: Escape clauses” (165), and across 300 lines never once said that a person may leave. A new paragraph now sits at 177, after the annulment note and downstream of indissolubility at 173, opening “Indissoluble has never meant that you must stay in the house.” CCC 1649, 2383 and 2386 are quoted verbatim and were verified against vatican.va before drafting. Five drafting constraints governed it and should govern any future edit to it: the permission gets its own unhedged sentence; no gatekeeping adjective the reader must measure herself against (a frightened person reading “only in extreme cases” concludes she does not qualify); the children are named, as CCC 2383 names them; separation is framed as protecting the persons covenant exists for, not as its failure; and the permission comes before the bond, because the one that comes first is the one she takes away. Do not soften, hedge or reorder this paragraph.

**The creation row was the one real doctrinal error.** Line 97's “God is our Creator—the same way our parents create us” made parental generation univocal with divine creation, which is exactly what CCC 366 exists to deny. Now: parents “give the body and the family; each soul is created directly by God Himself and is not ‘produced’ by the parents (CCC 366).” Line 99's hedge “(most immediately, but not on their own)” had the Catechism's own adverb pointing the wrong way — *immediately* belongs to God.

⚠ **Patrick's ruling: *author* is reserved for God.** Line 99's “authored that child's life” — pre-existing text, not a proposal — is now “gave that child life—truly, and never alone, since God alone is the Author of a soul.” The reservation is now made openly in the sentence, which does the work better than the hedge it replaced. Two other uses were checked and deliberately kept: line 117's novelist (“as the author”), which is the analogy that defines authorship and which the whole argument runs through, and line 133's “authored by humans,” the negative case where the word is being denied to us. Do not sweep those.

✗ **Rejected: `· RSV` on inline scripture citations.** The `wil-review-chapter` skill says to cite `Book Chapter:Verse · RSV`; the manuscript does not, anywhere. Its practice is the bare reference — (Jeremiah 31:33) at 103, (Matthew 5:17) at 220, (Proverbs 17:17) at 262. Two new quotations were drafted with the tag and Patrick had it removed. Scripture is still RSV and still quoted whole; only the tag is wrong. Do not re-add it, and do not take the skill file as authority against the manuscript's own practice.

**Row 1 was narrowed, and line 115 was already right.** Codex cited “115–149” and claimed authority was made to inhere only in an author. Line 115 reads “True authority is *inherent* only to the ‘author’ of the laws” — and *inherent* is precisely the word that makes the participated-authority distinction. Codex read past it. The actual error was the callout at 120, “Authority is only truly active when WE FREELY SUBMIT,” which the chapter contradicted at its own line 147: the toddler is bound by the stove rule and has submitted to nothing. Now “His authority holds whether we acknowledge it or not—but it does its work in us only when WE FREELY SUBMIT our will to His laws”; Patrick cut the original tail “since he is the Author” as redundant against the callout's own first sentence. A new paragraph after 117 states what the chapter never said out loud — that parental, ecclesial and civil authority is real, borrowed, binding, and ordered to the common good — with Romans 13:1 quoted whole. Lines 147 and 149 were swept in by the cited range and are both fine; 149's claim that the Gospel never *needed* force is about faith, and is CCC 160 and *Dignitatis Humanae*.

**Rows 2, 4 and 7 converged on one distinction:** the bond is indissoluble; the promises can be violated. Line 61's “unconditional” and “unbreakable” contradicted the chapter's own epigraph at line 10 (Jeremiah 31:32, “my covenant which they broke”) and its own lines 45 and 53. Now the gift is unconditional, the bond is permanent, and the promises can be broken without the bond being dissolved. Line 169 was carrying three rows at once and was redlined as one sentence: “we submit our lives to our spouse and children as we submit to Him” put *latria* language on a creature and now takes Ephesians 5:21's actual shape; “Marriage most fully fulfills our covenant with God” is backwards against CCC 1618–1619 and is now scoped to “for most people.” Line 175 gained the reason rather than an assertion: marriage belongs to this life (Matthew 22:30; CCC 1619, “a reality of this present age which is passing away”), which is *why* virginity signifies “the supremacy of the bond with Christ.” Widowhood, singleness and infertility are now named as not shutting anyone out.

But “sacred necessity” as a bare phrase in a callout, read first, lands on the individual reader, who may be a widow or a consecrated sister. Now “for the human race it is a sacred necessity.” **The natural-law clause in the same callout — “the law written on their hearts” — was left untouched deliberately:** the handoff named line 217 as one of the two places already stating the nature/grace distinction correctly, and it does. Both things were true of different sentences in the same callout.

✗ **Codex wrong about sourcing at line 137.** Row 6 asked for “precise historical causation and sources” at the paragraph that already carries footnote 2 — Courtois for the Soviet figure, Dikötter for the Chinese with its conservative-anchor reasoning stated, USHMM for the Nazi figure broken out by category — plus the charitable fence in its own text. Entry 37 holds this paragraph up as the model the Ch. 2 fix was rebuilt on. Codex did not read the footnote. Recorded so it is not raised a third time. What survived Row 6 was one word at 135: “imposed morality *inevitably* escalates” was a claimed historical law, unsourced and false as a universal; it is now “carries nothing in itself that can stop the escalation,” which is the logical claim the paragraph was actually making.

But it sits inside a clearly marked comparison doing rhetorical work. ### 38. ✅ Ch. 3 — triaged and revised (2026-09-17)

Six of the seven Codex rows had never been triaged (row 1 already carried a Claude DOWNGRADE, which was re-checked against the current text and stands). Ten changes applied after redline and approval; 5,987 → 6,160 words.

**The participation language was not swept.** It runs through roughly eighteen places and is the chapter's thesis, and much of it is defensible as written — “participation” carries a metaphysical sense (every real good holds its goodness from Goodness itself) that is ordinary Thomism. The exposure was the handful of places using the *deification* vocabulary — God's *life*, the divine *nature* — universally. So the distinction is now staged **once**, at line 153, where the chapter already quotes 2 Peter 1:3-4 and the verse is itself conditional (*through these promises* you *may become* partakers). That one addition licenses the metaphysical sense everywhere else, and the two callouts (130, 144) were adjusted because callouts are read first. The other twelve participation sentences were deliberately left alone. **Do not "finish the job" by sweeping them.**

Romans 5:5 remains in the chapter's Further Study.) Second, my replacement flattened his prose; his three closing sentences were restored nearly intact, with only the quantifier “When we love authentically” removed. **“We actually participate in it” survives** — once the distinction is drawn above it, the word is earned. That is the point of staging rather than sweeping.

**The Trinity row was promoted to first.** It sat sixth in the file. “The Spirit as fruit of love” (line 133) made the Holy Spirit the product of a process running between two others — now “the Spirit, who proceeds as Love and Gift.” Line 123's “each Person completely giving Himself to the others” flattened the relations of origin into three equals trading — now the Father gives all He is to the Son, the Son receives and returns it, the Spirit proceeds from both as the Love they share.

**Three findings Codex missed.** Line 111 carried “What reason discovers, revelation confirms” — the exact formula removed from Ch. 2 that morning, and after that fix the last instance in the manuscript; the chapter already contradicted it correctly at line 95 and in the callout at 98. Line 163's “Evil cannot even be described except as love refused” was the same privation overreach Ch. 2 line 57 had just been corrected for; now scoped to the evil persons choose. And the §18 sort recorded the night before was wrong (see the correction in entry 37).

✗ **Codex wrong twice.** Its straw-man charge against the materialist passage does not survive reading line 27, “This is not a foolish position. It deserves a serious response,” or line 31, which makes the very distinction Codex asks for. And holy/whole again — settled in Ch. 2; the wordplay at line 47 stands.

✅ **Codex right about something distinctively Catholic.** Line 175 made isolation a violation of our nature with no room for the eremitic life. CCC 920–921 describes hermits in “the silence of solitude,” their withdrawal “a silent preaching of the Lord.” The words *hermit*, *solitude* and *contemplative life* appeared nowhere in the manuscript, so the distinction was made nowhere. **Left alone, with reasons:** the “law requires a lawgiver” argument (line 83 argues rather than asserts, meets non-theistic moral realism head on, and defers to Ch. 12 — the cross-reference was verified to have survived the Ch. 11 renumber, `chapter_12.md` is still *The Lawgiver Is Love*); dignity at line 89 (the ontological ground is present, just late in a long paragraph); “sacrilege” at line 169 (stretched, not wrong — CCC 2120 does extend it to persons consecrated to God). Verified after writing: two blockquote wrappers, three callouts with their solarized inline styles, two `\hfill\small`, divs balanced, no footnote markers, no residue of any replaced phrase.

**Trinity orthodoxy pass, same session, at Patrick's request.** No heresy found. Verified sound: tritheism excluded by name at line 123; relations of origin now present; Filioque correct for the Latin tradition; “the one love that God is” (125) guards against three loves; “would name something He became rather than who He is” excludes a God who becomes; the Trinity correctly treated as revealed rather than reasoned to (CCC 237); CCC 257 quoted accurately; “not rival attributes inside God — they are one undivided love” is divine simplicity correctly stated; and the clause keeping suffering out of the divine nature holds, which is what the row 1 downgrade rests on.

⚠ **Four further fixes came out of that pass.** *“Love generates communion (the Spirit…)”* — **generation** is the technical verb for the Father–Son relation; the Spirit proceeds by spiration and is not a second Son, so the generation verb must not sit beside Him. Now “Love is life-giving,” which is also the canonical definition's own word. *Lines 135 and 149* were listed in the triage as needing the nature/grace staging and were then dropped from the redline without being flagged — my error. It matters because **staging only licenses what follows it**, and both sit before line 153; a reader met the strong universal claim twice before the distinction was drawn. Line 151 already had it right (“created with the *capacity to* participate”), so 149 was the odd one out even locally.

**One metaphor, chosen by the chapter itself.** Patrick asked why the replacement verbs (“flows from,” “reflecting,” “echoing”) were three different images. Line 115 already had the right one — “facets of a single reality, *lit from a single source*” — and *facets* is itself a light word; CCC 257 at line 127 says “unfading light.” The register is now *lit from* / *reflecting* / *reflects* throughout (115, 130, 135, 149). It also carries the doctrine without arguing it: **reflected light is real light** — genuinely light, genuinely derived. Prefer this image over abstract verbs wherever the nature/grace distinction needs making.

✅ **CCC 221 added at line 153:** “God himself is an eternal exchange of love, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and he has destined us to share in that exchange.” Two reasons it is the strongest sentence available there. Line 123's “an eternal exchange of perfect love” is *CCC 221's own wording*. And the Catechism stages nature and grace itself — not *we participate* but *he has destined us to share*; Patrick's 17 September ruling is CCC 221 in the Church's voice, which moves the staging from the author's argument to hers. The chapter had cited CCC 232–267 and 257 but not 221.

Ch. 3 at the close of that pass: **6,191 words** (later passes took it to 6,241 — see below). The audit file's Chapter 3 block carries nine rows, every one with a verdict, including the two findings Codex missed.

**Later the same week — three more passes on Ch. 3, all Patrick's catches.** *Line 153 tightened* (see the note above on Romans 5:5): seven sentences to four, two citations rather than three, the Scripture quotation untouched per §1. *Line 31, the missing rung:* the list climbed universe → physics → chemistry rich enough to build living cells → life that can reproduce, and never named the step where the cells started living. Added “a first crossing from inert mineral to living thing that no one has yet explained,” plus a clause making the logic airtight — selection *cannot reach back past the first living thing, since selection needs something already alive and reproducing before it can select at all.* That clause matters: without it the list reads as *science hasn't explained abiogenesis yet, therefore God*. With it the claim is about the shape of the mechanism, not the state of the evidence. **Deliberately not claimed: that abiogenesis is impossible.** The text says “no one has yet explained.” Do not strengthen it.

*Line 31 also gained Patrick's question:* why survival should count as a criterion at all. “Blind matter has no preference between holding together and falling apart. Selection can only reward survival in a world where something was already straining toward it.” That is finality in plain language — things tend toward their own good before anyone measures whether they got there — and it completes the contrast the paragraph already draws with mathematics, which cannot be disobeyed.

*Line 83, the lawgiver sentence.* Patrick proposed adding that moral law “creates something we describe as a law that we can voluntarily choose to submit to,” and ending with “something like an author who understands the personal nature of human beings.” The first half was adopted, the second declined and Patrick agreed: “something like” hedges two sentences after the chapter lands “A command requires a voice; a law requires a lawgiver,” and *understanding* persons is weaker than *being* personal — a gifted psychologist understands persons. Also, **“Author” already has a job in this chapter**: line 85 closes the problem-of-evil passage with “And that ache has an Author.” Final: “The moment we admit that moral truth genuinely binds persons—that it lays on us a law we can freely submit to or refuse—we have admitted that its source must be capable of binding persons, which is to say, personal.” The freedom clause completes the mathematics contrast (math cannot be disobeyed; moral law can) and ties to the book's free-will undercurrent.

⚠ *Line 89, the “unplanned” guard sentence — cut 2026-09-18, Patrick's catch.* The paragraph opened “Be careful here, though—the argument is not that something unplanned must be worthless. A child conceived by surprise is no less precious than a child long prayed for…” **Two faults in one sentence.** It answered an objection the paragraph never raised: observation three (line 87) is about who *confers* worth (“because we humans have decided it does”) — nothing there touches planning or how a thing came to exist; that guard belongs to the *first* observation, the unplanned-universe material at lines 25–31. And it was a **denial construction**, the same fault stripped from Ch. 2 at lines 103, 105 and the old 165 — it puts *unplanned = worthless* on the page and asks the reader not to think it.

**The decisive finding was not either fault — it was that the chapter had already answered this, at line 55.** *“You were an accident”* is named there as a desecration: “The child's very being has been called a mistake rather than a gift.” That meets the unplanned child where the wound is, thirty-four lines earlier and in far warmer language. Line 89's version was a second, colder answer to a settled question. **The paragraph also already had its child** — “the unloved child still has dignity—that is precisely why the neglect is so evil” — which is the load-bearing one; the child conceived by surprise arrived first and did no work. Both sentences were cut with nothing put in their place: line 87's “arbitrary preference” now runs straight into “The real question is what grounds that worth,” and *that worth* points back to *confer worth* in the preceding sentence. 6,283 → **6,241 words**; counts verified unchanged (2 blockquotes, 3 callouts, 2 `\hfill\small`, divs 5/5, no footnotes, no residue).

**General lesson, worth applying before any future rescue.** A first draft had re-anchored the sentence rather than cutting it (“Consider a child conceived by surprise…and nobody decided she would be”) — defensible, and it would have survived review. Patrick's question, *“but does it even need to be in this chapter?”*, is the one to ask first. **Before rescuing a sentence, check whether the book already answers it somewhere stronger, and whether the paragraph is carrying two images where only one is load-bearing.** The decision not to relocate the surviving line — *how a thing came to exist and what it is worth are different questions* — was deliberate: its only natural home is line 57, which makes the same point more warmly, and adding it there would cool the passage down. Do not move it there later.

✅ **Second arc, 2026-09-18 afternoon — Patrick asked the chapter to be tested rather than polished.** Four findings, all his prompts, and they compound.

*1. Line 109 said “the five observations argued from reason alone.” It is four.* The chapter states the four/one division correctly in three places — line 95 (“this final step leans on something the first four observations could not prove by themselves”), the callout at 98 (whose arrow chain has exactly four links), and line 111 — and wrongly in the one sentence that says the count out loud. Now: “the first four observations argued from reason alone, as if to a stranger, and the fifth took the Source's name on His own word.” **When a chapter asserts a count, check it against the chapter.**

*2. “God IS love” cut from the fourth observation (line 91), at Patrick's request.* It is the fifth observation's entire content; asserted in the fourth it spends the fifth's punch before the fifth arrives. It needed no new home — it already appears at 95 with the citation, in the callout at 98, and at 101. Nothing in the fourth observation's chain depended on it (the argument closes at “must flow from God's own unchanging, perfect nature”; the payoff rests on God's *being*, not His name), so the cut was clean. **The line to hold: the fourth observation may say what love requires; only the fifth may say what God is.** The word *love* elsewhere in the fourth stays — the callout at 98 opens its own reason-only chain with “love requires a personal source,” so reason works on love as experienced and what it cannot supply is the Source's *name*.

*3. The fourth observation's heading now names it as the completion of the second* — “that source must embody those values perfectly and unchangingly—or we have not escaped human opinion, only relocated it.” Thesis kept word for word so the callout at 98 still matches. Patrick asked whether to bring in Aquinas' Fourth Way here; **declined, and worth not revisiting**: its weak link (degrees → a maximum) is one line to rebut, defending it needs participation metaphysics, and it would swap the section's register from moral experience to abstraction. The Fourth Way's *conclusion* is already in the book three times (Ch. 2:51 and Ch. 3:103 *summum bonum*; Ch. 3:93 “He is Being itself, Goodness itself”). It now sits in Further Study only.

★ *4. Patrick's own argument, and the best thing to come out of the chapter.* He observed that when someone violates the moral law against us it **breaks our heart** — which is the phenomenology of a bond, not of a rule. Written into observation one: “We do not meet betrayal the way we meet a miscalculation. No one is wounded by a sum worked out wrong… what breaks is not a rule we were keeping, it is a bond we were inside.” **Guard the boundary:** this earns, by reason, that the law addresses persons and is violated as a bond. It does *not* earn that the Source is Love — that stays the fifth observation's revealed content. Do not let a later pass push it further. Patrick also raised that the good life is arguably scientifically demonstrable and said he does not want it in the book; **agreed, and for a reason worth keeping**: an argument that virtue correlates with flourishing hands the reader “so morality is just what promotes flourishing,” which is exactly what the second observation exists to refute.

✅ **St. John Henry Newman brought into the book — he appeared nowhere in seventeen chapters.** Declared a Doctor of the Church by Leo XIV on 1 November 2025, and his signature contribution is the argument this chapter makes. The *Grammar of Assent* (ch. 5) argues as Patrick does, from the felt texture of conscience rather than from the existence of moral facts: conscience excites “confusion, foreboding, self-condemnation,” therefore “There is One to whom we are responsible, before whom we are ashamed, whose claims upon us we fear.” Three placements: the *Grammar*'s mother sentence closes observation one; the *Letter to the Duke of Norfolk*'s conscience sentence closes line 109; both works are in Further Study, with CCC 1776-1778 and the Fourth Way.

★ **“Speaks to us behind a veil” is now the chapter's architecture.** Line 109 ends: *Reason hears the voice. Revelation lifts the veil.* That is the four-then-one structure in an image rather than in a claim, and it came from Newman rather than from argument. Prefer it over restating the division.

⚠ **Two corrections to my own recommendations, both worth remembering.** First, I proposed replacing observation one's “the real pain we feel when we lose a parent” because grief at loss is what evolutionary psychology explains best; Patrick said leave it. Newman then showed the better answer: not *losing* a parent but **hurting** one — “the same tearful, broken-hearted sorrow which overwhelms us on hurting a mother.” The parent was right to keep; it needed turning, not replacing. The clause became “the weight we feel when we have wronged someone who trusted us” so the paragraph does not carry two parent images. Second, I wanted *Gaudium et Spes* 16 inside observation three, where it states that observation almost verbatim (“a law which he does not impose upon himself”). **That would have broken the reason-alone register** the same session had just certified; it went to line 111 instead, which is past the handoff and already cites CCC 1954-1960.

⚠ **Patrick ruled on denial constructions, narrowing a rule I had been applying too widely.** “I am not opposed to all denial constructions.” He kept Newman's “Conscience is not a long-sighted selfishness, nor a desire to be consistent with oneself” — and it belongs at line 109, because the objection at 107 is *“You're just projecting human values onto God,”* and those two denials answer projection precisely. **The working rule: deny what the reader has actually said, never what he might have thought.** What made the Ch. 2 cases bad was Patrick denying something about his own argument — planting a doubt in order to wave it away. Answering a stated objection is not planting one.

Ch. 3 after both arcs: **6,558 words**, 219 lines; 2 blockquotes, 3 callouts, 2 `\hfill\small`, divs 5/5, no footnotes. Pillar lists verified Oxford-comma-free in all four places. *Earned* (47, 61) and *transaction* (65) appear pre-existing and in the negated sense (what the parent-child bond is *not*), not the atonement sense the §1 rule guards; left alone and noted here so a later pass does not re-flag them as new.

### 37. ✅ Ch. 2 — nature and grace settled, and the bishop-readiness revision applied (2026-09-17)

Patrick ruled the nature/grace question the audit's “119, 155–169” row turns on, in two stages. **Nature:** God writes the orientation toward the good into every soul, inescapably; the atheist who loves his child, disciplines him in justice, forgives him in mercy and sacrifices to provide for him is really doing those things, aimed at goods that are perceived, limited and incomplete. Even the man arguing against God orients himself toward something he takes to be good. **Grace:** when the Source is recognised, God draws the person into His own love and reorients them toward what is actually good — true justice, true mercy, true sacrifice.

This is not new doctrine for the book; it is already stated at Ch. 1 line 43 (natural law written on every human heart, Rom 2:14-15 in Further Study), Ch. 4 lines 105 and 217, Ch. 6 lines 61 and 73, Ch. 7 line 39, and most precisely at Ch. 7 line 67 — “not because non-believers can't recognize justice (natural law allows this), but because they can't” ground it. Chapters 2 and 3 were the two that drifted into unstaged participation language. The finding is an internal inconsistency, not a theological correction.

**The governing rule, for Ch. 3 and the rest of the participation register:** stage-two sentences keep *participates* and *shares in His life*; stage-one sentences take *reflects*, *images*, *is written into*, *comes from*.

⚠ **Corrected 2026-09-17, later the same day.** This entry originally continued: “Ch. 3 lines 135 and 149 read correctly as they stand. Ch. 3 lines 128, 169 and 173 are stage one and need the other verb.” **That sentence-by-sentence sort was wrong, and it was written without having read Chapter 3** — the line numbers were taken from the audit annotation and the sort was assumed. On reading the chapter: the line numbers had drifted (the callout the audit calls 128 is at 130; “the Spirit as fruit of love” it calls 130 is at 133); the sort was backwards in part (135 and 149 are among the *clearest* instances — “we’re sharing in God’s own life,” “We’re participating in the very life of God”); and the scale was more than double what was recorded — roughly eighteen places, not eight. Do not trust a per-line sort in this file that was not made against the chapter text.

⚠ The triage's narrowing of that row was wrong by one line. It cleared lines 119 and 155 together and justified that by quoting “if love doesn't come from God … everything else collapses” — which is line 155's text, not line 119's. Line 119 rested a stage-two claim (“participation in God's life”) on a stage-one ground (“because every person is created in God's image”). Check that a verdict's supporting quotation actually belongs to the line it clears.

**Ch. 2 line 151 — deletion proposed and overruled.** The first redline proposed cutting “the ‘west’ has conquered much evil, but still has much to do.” Patrick rejected it: Christian influence really did lead people to pursue what is good — honest dealing in commerce, moral education, resistance to tyranny — and he stands by the claim. The finding was misdiagnosed. The defect was asymmetry, not the thesis: Ch. 4 line 137 argues the negative half of the same case with three figures, a footnote and an immediate charitable fence, while Ch. 2 gave the positive half eight scare-quoted words. Rewritten on the Ch. 4 pattern, with *Christianity* as the subject rather than “the West” (which drags in colonialism the point does not need). **Do not re-propose the deletion.**

⚠ Verification caught two bad historical examples before they reached the page. The widely repeated claim that the Council of Nicaea (325) directed bishops to establish hospitals does not hold up in available sources — dropped. Ambrose requiring Theodosius' penance after Thessalonica (390) is real, but the cathedral-door scene is a later invention of Theodoret's and the “Church over State” reading is disputed by modern scholarship — dropped as too contested to carry a claim. What survived, and is now the chapter's first footnote: the Basiliad (c. 372), Bologna (1088) and Paris (mid-twelfth century) grown from Church schools, the School of Salamanca on just price and restitution, and *Mit brennender Sorge* (issued 10 March 1937, read from German pulpits 21 March). Check historical examples against sources before drafting them, not after.

✗ Rejected vocabulary: **imputed / imputation**, added to the §1 Never-use list. Patrick used it in conversation to describe the orientation God places in the soul. It is the Reformation's forensic term (Trent VI, canon 11) and also the wrong word for original sin, which is contracted rather than reckoned (CCC 404–405) — the distinction the September Ch. 1 revision already navigated. The book's phrase is “written on the heart.” The word appears nowhere in the manuscript.

**Applied to chapter_02.md: twelve edits of thirteen proposed.** Patrick kept “They are ‘Holy’ (wholly)” — and note Codex was *wrong* that holy/whole is a folk etymology: Old English *hālig* derives from *hāl*, the root of hale, heal and health. Reason/revelation fixed at the heading (line 75) and the callout (line 86), with line 77's knock-on premise. Line 55 moved the ultimate good from love to communion with God. Patrick had them removed the same day: a blind reader meets the word *evil* in the same sentence as “blindness lacks sight,” and the technical sense of “physical evil” is not the sense a lay reader carries. Do not reintroduce them, or any bodily condition, as an illustration of privation. The concession is now stated rather than illustrated (“Which good is missing depends on what has been lost”), the moral-evil scope is named before the claim about love rather than in a later aside, and the actual Thomistic precision was never in the examples — it is in “where love is *owed* and withheld,” which is untouched. Chapter 2 is 3,500 words.

Verified after writing: two blockquote wrappers, three callout wrappers with their solarized inline styles, two `\hfill\small`, all divs balanced, one footnote marker against one note defined, the canonical definition byte-identical, and no residue of any replaced phrase.

**Four further rounds the same day, each redlined and approved separately.** *Line 57 again:* the broken-bone/blindness pair came out (see the rejected-illustration note above). *Lines 103 and 105:* Patrick judged that the passage devalued Augustine, Aquinas and the Greek tradition — reading as though they had not managed to define love and this book would. The applied version praises the tradition plainly, opens no comparison, and makes *love* the subject of every sentence about the difficulty — “Love will exceed this definition as it exceeds every other,” not “my definition falls short too,” since *too* concedes a shortfall by grouping it with theirs. “Crazy little thing called love” went out with the sentence it lived in (a Queen title, and out of register beside the definition). *“A many-splendored thing”* is now attributed to **Francis Thompson** (1859–1907), the English Catholic poet of *The Hound of Heaven*, from his poem *The Kingdom of God* — verified, and used as a bare attribution rather than a verse quotation.

*The Bridge to Sacred:* Patrick asked whether line 167 should move into the Bridge. It should, and for a reason bigger than the duplication: every other Bridge in the book is a short forward pointer to the next chapter (Ch. 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 all checked), while Ch. 2's stated a thesis and handed off to nothing — and line 167 (“We begin with the first word of our definition: sacred. His shorter version stands, with one sentence added to restore the resurrection, which the cut had removed from the one section chapter_01.md line 81 defers to by name: “And a Love that outlasts everything that can hurt you: the resurrection of the body, and the life of the world to come.” Final: **3,507 words**.

### 36. ✅ Ch. 2 — the audit block triaged, before any editing (2026-09-17)

**Chapter 2 was the one chapter whose audit findings were never triaged.** Its block in `what-is-love-bishop-readiness-audit-2026-08-26-claude.html` was byte-identical to the Codex original — zero `Claude ·` annotations, seven raw Codex rows. Chapter 1 had six. That gap is now closed: all ten rows carry a verdict (4 UPHOLD, 1 DOWNGRADE, 1 MODIFY, 1 CODEX WRONG, 3 ADDED), written into the audit file in the same markup as every other chapter. **`chapter_02.md` itself was not touched** — the triage is a set of proposals, and Patrick has not reviewed the verdicts.

**⚠ A trap this uncovered: the “Cleared” row is Codex clearing itself.** Chapter 2’s “infinite dignity / *Dignitas Infinita*” row appears in both audit files. It reads like a reviewer ruling and is not one. A draft prompt written this day cited it as “cleared by me,” which would have given a fresh session false authority for it. **Check both files before attributing any row to a reviewer.** Only rows carrying `Claude ·` are annotations.

**The chapter’s worst exposure, and Codex located it loosely.** The callout at `chapter_02.md` line 86 reads “What reason discovers, Scripture confirms: God is love,” and the section heading at line 75 says the same. Natural reason reaches God’s existence and some attributes; “God is love” in its full sense is Trinitarian and revealed. **The chapter already knows this** — line 51 says *revelation* confirms who that God is — so it contradicts itself, and the wrong version sits in a callout and a heading, which is where a censor looks. The fix is narrow: “reason discovers” is correct for *love is the highest human good* and wrong for *God is love*.

**Three findings Codex missed, one of them consequential.** `chapter_02.md` line 19 recaps Chapter 1 as “abortion as contraception, children mutilated by gender ideology, media lies destroying truth,” while Chapter 1’s own vignettes say “She’s not cruel. She genuinely believes this is the good choice” and “He is not malicious.” **Leaving it partly cancels the 2026-09-09 Chapter 1 revision**, because a reviewer reading the two in sequence sees the charity of Chapter 1 undone by its own summary one page later. Also: *A Note on Natural Evil* at line 159 sits after the chapter’s closing beat at line 157 (“Let’s begin.”) and should move before line 155 — but must not be cut or weakened, since `chapter_01.md` line 81 defers natural evil to it by name and that deferral is why the Chapter 1 Argument finding was downgraded. And line 163 does pillar interplay in a body section, restating all four pillars twice in one paragraph, which §1 reserves to the Binding Check.

**✗ Codex is wrong about holy/whole.** Its Copy row calls the wordplay at line 115 a popular simplification with no etymological basis. Old English *hālig* (“holy”) derives from *hāl* (“whole, sound, healthy”), the same root as *hale*, *heal* and *health*. The pun has a genuine basis in English. It still proves nothing about God and may go on those grounds, but it must not be described as an error.

**Two Codex findings are misquoted, and one nearly cost a real finding.** Codex quotes “The West conquered much evil”; line 151 actually reads *the “west” has conquered much evil, but still has much to do* — lowercase, in scare quotes. And Codex flags “sacrifice proves love”, a phrase not in the chapter; a draft prompt therefore told the next session to drop the finding, when its real referent is line 133, “Love proves itself through action.” **A phrase Codex quotes may be a paraphrase. Search for the idea before concluding the finding is groundless.**

**Also recorded:** the “circular reasoning” row buries the better finding inside the weaker one — privation is of a *due* good (a broken bone lacks integrity, blindness lacks sight), so line 57’s “the absent good is love” overreaches; while the circularity charge is already answered by line 73 (“That is not a theorem; it is a verdict”). And the line 169 fix — “love must be sacred, or it is nothing at all” collapsing natural love into supernatural participation — is the same error family as the upheld `chapter_03.md:128` finding. **Decide the two together when Chapter 3 is taken up.**

### 35. ✅ Ch. 1 — bishop-readiness revision applied over two rounds (2026-09-09)

Nineteen changes to `chapter_01.md` plus one to `chapter_06.md`. The chapter went from 2,980 to 3,176 words. Two footnotes added; the chapter's five notes became seven.

**The two downgrades in Patrick's audit redline were verified and both hold.** Line 73 supplies the *viator* distinction in so many words, so only the bolded aphorism at line 71 needed "For a creature still on the way to God." And **the Chapter 2 cross-reference, never checked before, is kept**: `chapter_02.md` line 159 is a section headed *A Note on Natural Evil* which concedes the Church "has never claimed to hold a formula that dissolves the mystery of suffering," grounds that in CCC 309, and closes on the resurrection of the body. Chapter 1's parenthesis at line 81 is honest. Do not reopen either.

**Amended 2026-09-10 — the paragraph at line 73 is no longer word for word, and the reason matters.** The *viator* distinction is untouched; it lives in "freedom fulfilled" and "cannot be installed at the start," and those are unchanged. What changed is the two sentences after them. Patrick raised the objection himself: **the paragraph as written implied a works-based salvation.** "That fullness … is the fruit of a love freely given and freely kept, day after day, until it is complete" made beatific freedom the product of a sustained effort, with duration sounding like a requirement, and this session's proposed replacement for the closing sentence ("it is how a soul grows large enough to hold it") was worse, making the walking the *mechanism* of the capacity. **The test that settles it is the Good Thief** — no time, no means, nothing to show, and "today you will be with me in Paradise." Baptized infants who die are the same test from the other end, and CCC 2010 is explicit that no one merits the initial grace of justification. Any sentence Dismas falsifies has to go.

**The fix was to move the requirement off duration and onto consent.** What God will not compel is a *yes*, and a yes is a single act, not a career. Now reads: "That fullness cannot be installed at the start, because a love that was never freely given is not love at all. God waits for a yes He could have compelled and would not." The paragraph's actual job — answering why God did not create us already confirmed in glory — is unaffected, and the reason now rests on the nature of love rather than on a process.

**✗ Rejected — adding the Good Thief to this paragraph.** A draft ended "And the yes need not take a lifetime: the thief beside Him had one sentence left, and it was enough." Patrick asked whether it could safely be removed; it can, and cutting it is the better edit. Three reasons, recorded so it is not re-added: the works exposure is already closed by the two sentences above it, so it carries nothing; the paragraph never asked the deathbed question, and answering an unasked question is the same wandering that condemned the sentence it replaced; and **standing alone in a chapter with no other treatment of justification, "one sentence was enough" gives no hint that the thief's yes was itself grace-given** — the mirror error, cheap grace instead of works, and an unguarded gift to a reader coming from the other direction. Dismas belongs where contrition and the deathbed sacraments are actually discussed; `chapter_08.md` already has that ground in the Anointing of the Sick section (see item 34).

Also amended the same day: the sentence "The road of freedom must be walked for the arrival to be an arrival" was cut as a tautology — it says only that one must travel in order to have travelled, which reads as profound once and evaporates on a second pass.

**The sin callout — Patrick's own formulation, not the audit's fix.** The proposed replacement was set aside in favour of his: "A simple way to say it: sin is choosing a lesser good over the greatest Good." The framing is what actually closed the finding, because it stops the callout competing with CCC 1849 and 1440 and lets it be the mnemonic he always wanted. Lesser/greatest is Augustine's own and covers what the old line could not — blasphemy, omission, sin against oneself. **The capital on "Good" is deliberate and load-bearing:** Patrick's stated aim was a sentence a non-theist could accept, and the capital costs that reader nothing while keeping God present in a callout sitting thirty lines above "Sin is before all else an offense against God." Patrick delegated the call to this session. If it is ever lowercased, the audit finding reopens and should be recorded as open. The following paragraph was repaired to match: "Consider 'the good' versus 'a perceived good'" became "Consider a lesser good versus the greatest Good."

**The organizer vignette, de-racialized without being softened.** "She has seen real racism. She has buried real victims." and both *never* sentences keep their shape — Patrick rejected the added framing as a distinction without a difference, correctly, since the vignette already grants her everything with "she isn't making excuses." Two changes carried weight: the race-specific statistic became the national one (close to one child in four, roughly 19 million, Census and Annie E. Casey), and the policy claim narrowed from "policies that made single motherhood financially rational" — the Moynihan-to-Murray thesis, which the literature does not settle — to what is documented and citable, that marriage can cost a low-income household money (Congressional Research Service R49020; Congressional Budget Office, *Effective Marginal Tax Rates for Low- and Moderate-Income Workers*). A third new note sources the school-secrecy claim to California's SAFETY Act, Assembly Bill 1955 of 2024, a statute rather than a news story, so it will not go stale.

**✗ Rejected by Patrick — the Romans 6:23 finding, and this session was wrong to raise it.** "The wages of sin is death" at line 37 was flagged as a breach of the §1 full-and-verbatim rule. It is not. That rule came from item 27 and targets *adapted or composited* quotations; a complete clause, quoted verbatim and accurately cited, with the whole verse blockquoted fifty lines later at the head of the next section, is ordinary citation practice. Line 37 is untouched, "So true." included. Do not re-raise it.

**✗ Rejected — qualifying "To demand a world without evil."** The line-71 qualifier plus the paragraph at line 73 already carry it.

**Also applied.** "Each generation inherits brokenness as their birthright" became "What was handed to them, they hand on, until grace interrupts it," which fixes both the inherited-guilt reading (original sin is contracted, not committed — CCC 404–405) and the determinism, and puts the chapter's only mention of grace into its darkest paragraph. *Sin: The Root of All Evil* became *The Root of Moral Evil*, matching CCC 310 and Chapter 2's own scoping, with "every form of moral evil" at line 63. The pornography claim moved off neuroscience and onto morals, in Patrick's own wording ("see an object to be used"). Politics, Education and Scientism were each de-overstated. The atheist sentence was rebuilt without its false dilemma and now opens "The atheist who rages against evil is right to rage." "We refuse to use them" became "we, wounded and often unwilling, do not reach for them." Romans 2:15 de-duplicated. *Why Man-Made Solutions Fall Short* hyphenated; *The Bridge to the Answer*, matching the house pattern, which names a concept and never a chapter title. Plus heading case, one comma splice, two stray commas and one agreement error.

**Ch. 6 line 99 — one sentence, and it removed an inconsistency between chapters.** Chapter 1's "science has nothing to say about why we choose evil" flatly contradicted Chapter 6, which credits science with "discovering truth about the physical world." Chapter 1 now tracks Chapter 6's *what* and *how* against *why there is anything to ask about*. Separately Patrick asked that Ch. 6 be more precise: science discovers truth about the physical world but not all truth, and is one tool among many. **The first half was already in the sentence** — "for discovering truth about the physical world" states the scope outright; only the second was missing. Inserted: "It is also one tool among several, and the physical world is not the whole of what can be known: mathematics, history, philosophy and the testimony of witnesses each reach truths no laboratory is built to test." Those four are chosen, not decorative — mathematics is the hardest counterexample to dispute, history is knowledge of unrepeatable particulars which is the shape of the Resurrection claim, philosophy is where the next sentence's presuppositions get examined, and "the testimony of witnesses" points at revelation without naming it, keeping the paragraph followable by an unbeliever to its end.

**✗ Rejected — "science is not the study of truth."** It contradicts that paragraph's own opening clause and hands a scientifically literate censor a free objection in the chapter that most needs his trust. What the paragraph already argues is stronger: science reaches real truths, and every one of them rests on truths science did not establish and cannot.

### 34. ✅ Ch. 8 — the Reformation passage, kept but reframed (2026-09-05)

The last open item from the Codex audit's ecumenism findings, and the one this session raised as an added finding the audit missed. `chapter_08.md` line 217, closing the section on the Anointing of the Sick.

**Was:** "This is one of the most pastorally devastating losses in most all of the communities born of the Reformation — and certainly in the modern 'evangelical' movement. There is no bedside sacrament, no anointing, no absolution, no Viaticum — only words and presence, however well-meant."

**Now:** "Not every Christian community kept this. Where the bedside sacraments were let go, what remains at the deathbed is words and presence, offered in real love but not the thing itself: no anointing, no absolution, no Viaticum."

**Patrick chose to keep the contrast** (Draft A) over the alternative that removed it entirely and stated the Catholic gift positively (Draft B, which this session recommended). His reason, given privately and *deliberately not written into the book at his instruction*: he witnessed a death in his own family with no priest and no prayers. That matters for how the passage should be understood by anyone editing it later — it is not a polemical flourish but a report of something he watched, which is a fair answer to the objection that it argues past the reader.

**What the reframing fixed, and why it was needed even keeping the claim.** Three defects, all real: (a) §1 forbids naming Protestant traditions and forbids comparative framing — both names are gone; (b) "most all of the communities born of the Reformation" was *factually loose*, since Lutherans and Anglicans retain anointing of the sick and some Lutheran bodies practise individual confession and absolution, so a reader who knew that would find the sentence overreaching in the same breath it named them, costing the true part; (c) "in most all of" is not English, in one of the chapter's most affecting passages. The new wording also supplies the steelman §1 requires — "offered in real love" — while still saying plainly that something is missing.

**Book-wide check after applying:** no remaining instance of "the Reformation," "evangelical movement," or any named Protestant tradition framed comparatively, in any chapter. The two §1 breaches this session found (Ch. 8 here, and the Introduction's Methodist paragraph, where naming was separately approved as the author's own testimony reporting recorded public votes) are now the only places a tradition is named at all.

### 33. ✅ Introduction — full revision applied over five review rounds (2026-09-05)

Seventeen changes to `3_introduction.md` plus one to `chapter_10.md`, worked through five rounds of rich-HTML review. The chapter went from 3,238 to 4,022 words, most of it the reworked testimony and a new four-note footnote block (the Introduction previously had none).

**The structural find neither audit caught.** The Introduction promised a *two*-part book (*The Nature of Perfect Love*, Ch. 1–10; *The Test of Love*, Ch. 11–17). The book actually builds *four*, with four different names. Patrick: "the four printed parts of course." Now: Part I The Question and the Answer (1–2), Part II The Facets of Perfect Love (3–10), Part III Living Love and Its Failures (11–16), Part IV Love Fulfilled in Christ (17). `chapter_10.md`'s "This is where Part 2 begins" corrected to Part III — an error introduced by this session's own earlier edit and caught later.

**The Methodist testimony, rewritten on the record rather than on assertion.** Replaced "Lies about human sexuality within the Methodist Church" with the documented votes: 2019 special session 438–384 to keep the teaching; 2024 General Conference striking "incompatible with Christian teaching" and lifting the clergy ban 692–51; more than 7,600 congregations gone under ¶2553. **Naming the communion was explicitly approved by Patrick** as an exception to the §1 rule, on the grounds that it is his own former communion, in his own testimony, reporting recorded public votes. A third naming was still trimmed from the closing sentence, because at that point reporting turns into indictment. Closes with a pointer to Ch. 6.

*Fact-check that changed the argument:* Patrick asked whether the Wesleyan Quadrilateral is Scripture/tradition/reason/experience. It is — but the term is Albert Outler's from the 1960s, not Wesley's, and **Scripture is primary within it**, so the original line "Truth had not been consulted first" was unfair as written. Outler later regretted coining the term precisely because it was read as four equal authorities. The paragraph now argues the stronger and more charitable point: four inputs with no living authority to settle them cannot hold when they disagree.

**⚠ The BLM quotation was wrong and was corrected before it reached disk.** The draft read "disrupt the Western-prescribed nuclear family structure." The actual text, which Patrick verified by pasting the April 2020 capture, ends "…nuclear family structure **requirement**." Dropping that word turns "we oppose the expectation that families take this form" into "we oppose families" — a truncation at exactly the word that changes the meaning, and the kind of thing that discredits a whole chapter. The paragraph now quotes in full and argues the ground that actually holds: the phrase *Western-prescribed*, treating the family as a cultural prescription rather than something given. **Standing lesson: never truncate a hostile quotation without seeing the full sentence.**

Patrick's instruction was to keep all three of his original claims but convert the two unsourced ones to observation language, which is what the paragraph now does. Sourced additions: Verisk/PCS on 2020 insured losses exceeding \$2 billion across 140 cities in 20 states; and, at his suggestion, the defence of looting in print and on public radio (Osterweil, *In Defense of Looting*, 2020). *Named the argument, not the author, in the body text.* No death count was used — no citable figure could be verified.

**Voice and claim-scope changes.** "The interpretive key we've been missing" dropped in both places as too dogmatic (Patrick). The humility callout rebuilt around his own note to the editor — "a more cohesive view of what the Church has been teaching all along" — which answers the DC-01 objection better than any hedge, because it says the definition organizes the deposit rather than adding to it. "When we read" → "when I read" (testimony, not assumed agreement). "Birthright as children of God" → "the very life God offers them as His children." "The Scriptures begin to open in their totality" → "stop reading like many books and start reading like one story" — Patrick flagged "totality" as overclaiming. The prayer sentence replaced because he would not actually pray daily and did not want to say so.

Also applied: Ch. 13 blurb (initial justification is a real moment; "every virtue" softened), Ch. 15 blurb (the "incomplete love isn't love at all" clause removed entirely at Patrick's instruction, which went further than the proposed softening), the three-line display of the canonical definition with its four ornamental em-dashes removed, "we specifically chose" → "I specifically chose", and two double spaces.

Verified after writing: three `\hfill`, three blockquote divs, one callout, divs balanced, four footnote markers with four notes defined, canonical definition byte-identical, no residue of superseded text.

**Rounds 6–7, after Patrick re-read the revised chapter.** Eleven further notes, all resolved. Verbatim fixes he authored: "admittedly a more superficial love"; "good and faithful youth from good Christian families"; "the *sacrificial* work of *actual* justice"; counterfeits that lead "themselves, their families and our society" astray; "a *good* understanding of what love is"; "It has *illuminated* my understanding"; "The Answer to *the Problem of* Evil"; "perfectly *fulfills* every facet."

**⚠ A continuity break this session introduced, and fixed.** Expanding one paragraph into eight stranded "I noticed something profound: sincere, well-meaning Methodists on both sides…" five paragraphs downstream, so the reader left the Methodists, passed through the riots and the looting, and was returned to a Methodist observation with no signal. Patrick's note read as a request for more precision; the actual defect was position. The paragraph was *moved* up to sit directly after the 2024 vote, where it feeds the conclusion instead of trailing it. Nothing was rewritten. *Lesson: when a paragraph is expanded substantially, check what used to follow it.*

**✗ Declined:** Patrick's suggestion to add, in that same sentence, that Methodists were "joining the BLM movement." "Both sides" there means the two sides of the sexuality question, each claiming Scripture — BLM is not a side of that question, so it changes the subject inside the sentence rather than sharpening it; the characterization is unsourced; and it would add a fourth category to a passage that is defensible precisely because organization, movement and rioters are kept distinct. Patrick accepted.

**The book's method, stated once in the opening.** New line after "What is Love?": "Much of what I understand about love, I learned by contrast — from watching what is plainly not good for people and asking what was missing." A first draft using "I learned much of this backwards" was rejected by Patrick as not what he meant; his own framing is the contrast between who God is and "the chaotic flailing of society fighting for justice without truth or mercy or love." This sentence tells the reader early why the book keeps examining counterfeits.

**Two cuts.** The "This is not the salvation the Bible teaches" paragraph removed (Patrick: "getting into the arguments"), with the following sentence repaired, since its pronoun pointed back at the deleted text — "How did we lose sight of ~~this transformative vision~~ the transformation salvation is meant to be?" And **The Journey Ahead cut from 713 words to 132**, keeping the four parts with one line each and dropping every per-chapter blurb. Patrick's objection was spoilers; the additional argument for it is that *those blurbs were where two doctrinal errors had been hiding* — the Ch. 13 "not a single moment" and the Ch. 15 "incomplete love isn't love at all," both flagged by the audit. A summary that compresses a chapter into a sentence keeps generating overstatements, and a censor reads every line of it. The 1 Thessalonians epigraph now closes the section rather than interrupting Part III.
