### 32. ✗ REJECTED — tying BLM to Marxism/wokeism, and a racism counterfeit (2026-09-05)

Both considered at length and both declined by Patrick. Recorded so neither is reopened cold.

**✗ Naming the Marxism–wokeism–BLM lineage: rejected. Leave it implicit.** Ch. 15's Wokeism entry already carries the structural argument in its own words — "Marxism recast for a modern audience: the same story of oppressor and oppressed, with race, sex, and identity standing in for economic class. The target has moved; the machinery has not." That is the theological work; naming the organization as an instance would add recognition, not explanatory power. The Introduction stays testimony plus the Ch. 16 pointer.

*Available if ever wanted, verified 2026-09-05 but deliberately unused:* co-founder Patrisse Cullors, in a 2015 interview with Jared Ball on the Real News Network, said of herself and Alicia Garza "We are trained Marxists. We are super-versed on, sort of, ideological theories." If it is ever used, it describes the *founders' self-understanding* only — stretching it to the marchers repeats the organization/movement/rioters conflation.

*Also corrected in passing:* Patrick's working assumption that BLM was "an outgrowth of wokeism" is backwards chronologically — BLM launched in 2013 and is one of the tributaries that fed what was later called wokeism. He agreed the argument does not need a claim about which came first. Do not reintroduce one.

**✗ Racism as a thirteenth Ch. 15 counterfeit: rejected.** Proposed by Patrick, then declined by him after seeing the cost ("no i dont want to add another counterfeit"). The *gap it would have closed is real and remains open*, and is recorded here rather than argued again: **the word "racism" appears nowhere in the manuscript.** Ch. 7 has "Partiality" and "Dehumanization" as concepts; Ch. 1 has a community-organizer vignette. So the book critiques a movement founded against racism, and critiques wokeism, without ever naming the evil those were responding to. A diocesan reviewer may ask about that. Patrick has weighed it and decided; do not re-propose the counterfeit entry.

**The governing consideration behind both.** The more the four-facet framework is welded to named political organizations, the more the book reads as a political tract rather than catechesis — which is the central risk both the Codex audit and this review identified. The theological argument is the load-bearing material; the political examples are cargo.

**⚠ Correction (2026-09-09) — the factual premise stated above is wrong.** This item records that "the word *racism* appears nowhere in the manuscript." It appears in four places: `chapter_01.md` line 25 ("She has seen real racism"); `chapter_07.md` line 264, where racism is named inside the *Dehumanization* entry as an offence against justice, with CCC 1700 and 1934–1938 and *Evangelium Vitae* behind it; `chapter_07.md` line 163 ("anti-racism"); and the Introduction at lines 38 and 44 ("racial justice," "racial injustice"). **The decision stands and is better supported on the corrected facts, not worse** — a diocesan reviewer who asks where the book addresses racism has an answer in the Justice chapter. ### 31. ✅ Ch. 6 — the *rule of truth* anchor, and the word-count rule retired (2026-09-05)

**Applied to `chapter_06.md`,** inside the closing paragraph of *Truth and Authority*, three sentences after "…the sign Christ Himself chose to give the world that He was sent by the Father":

> Make unity the goal, and one day you must call two opposite answers both true. The price is the truth. The Church has measured herself instead by what Irenaeus, writing around the year 180, called the *rule of truth* — the faith received from the apostles, which she "guards with care, as dwelling in but a single house, and similarly believes as if having but one soul and a single heart" (CCC 173).

**Why here and why so small.** The chapter already made the argument — Christ "did not pray that His disciples would agree to disagree," the Church is pillar of the truth "not because she *creates* truth, but because she *receives* it," the deposit guarded whole "because it was given, not deduced," and the Judges refrain as the picture of a body with no binding authority. What was missing was the name and the pedigree. Placed after that sentence rather than earlier because the "did not pray … / He prayed …" pair is a rhetorical unit; placed before "A divided Christianity preaches a divisible Christ" so it runs straight into the existing paragraph on the Church's authority serving "not truth alone but the integration of truth with justice, mercy and sacrifice."

**Cited inline as (CCC 173), deliberately not as a footnote.** Ch. 6's notes run 1–6 and note 5 falls at line 290, past the insertion; a new footnote here would have been note 5 and forced renumbering two markers and two note lines. CCC 173 quotes Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* 1, 10, 1–2, under the Catechism's own heading "Only One Faith."

**Deliberately excluded:** any naming of the Methodists (§1 rule — and generic is the better writing, since it indicts a *structure* that any body can fall into rather than a communion); Patrick's bishop anecdote (withdrawn by him, since the Commission on a Way Forward's published mandate — to "explore options that help to maintain and strengthen the unity of the church" — makes the same point and is citable); and any pillar-interplay line, since **§1 reserves pillar interplay to the Binding Check**, which already covers truth without justice / mercy / sacrifice.

**★ Word-count rule retired (Patrick, 2026-09-05).** `AGENTS.md` line 11 read "**Length:** 2,000–2,500 words per chapter" — the source every review had been measuring against, including the finding that Ch. 6 was "3.5× over." Patrick: "we will not try to solve any length issues … i am happy with their lengths." Replaced with no target and no ceiling, judged by robustness and proportion. Note that `memory.html` §1 already said this; `AGENTS.md` was the stale copy. **Still outstanding:** the `wil-review-chapter` skill also carries "Chapters run 2,000–2,500 words" and will keep reintroducing the constraint until its saved copy is corrected.

"the absolute necessity and" cut from that sentence as reading oddly (Patrick).

The line that must stay bright is narrower than the Codex audit drew it: **"inspiration" in the technical sense — the charism by which the Holy Spirit is author of Sacred Scripture — is reserved to Scripture and to nothing else**. Devotional language about God disclosing Himself to a soul was never the problem. The distinction that decided ¶17 was not the word but what it governs: revelation attached to *the author's experience of God* is fine; revelation attached to *the manuscript's content* is the claim the Preface disclaims.

### 27. ✅ Scripture edition corrected to RSV in the front matter (2026-08-29)

**The manuscript was already quoting RSV; only the label was wrong.** `1_frontmatter.md` named the Revised Standard Version, Second Catholic Edition (RSV-2CE), published by Ignatius Press. But the quoted text throughout is plain RSV — diagnostic: Ch. 6 quotes John 17:17–23 as "Sanctify them in the truth; *thy* word is truth. As *thou didst* send me…" and Psalm 119:160 as "the sum of *thy* word is truth." RSV retains archaic second-person pronouns in address to God; RSV-2CE deliberately removed exactly those. The text matches the §1 standing rule (RSV, always); the notice did not.

**Why the distinction matters.** RSV is licensed by the National Council of Churches through Friendship Press, whose gratis-use policy permits up to 500 verses with no written permission and no fee — only the prescribed notice. RSV-2CE is Ignatius Press's edition; their guideline treats roughly 500 *words* as fair use and asks that permission be secured before release, with fees possible. Mislabelling the book as RSV-2CE would have obliged a licence request it does not need.

**Applied:** the Scripture notice now reads the wording prescribed by the licensor — "Scripture quotations are from the Revised Standard Version of the Bible, copyright © 1946, 1952, and 1971 the Division of Christian Education of the National Council of the Churches of Christ in the United States of America. Used by permission. All rights reserved."

**New standing rule (Patrick, 2026-08-29):** Scripture is always quoted *in full and verbatim* — never adapted, shortened, or composited. The sentence "Some quotations have been adapted or shortened for readability" has been removed from the front matter, which means any adapted quotation still in the text is now a defect to be restored to verbatim RSV. See Future Task \#26 for the verse count, and the separate sweep for adapted quotations.

**Corrected two errors in the Codex bishop-readiness audit** while verifying this: the audit stated that the front matter asserts "Used with Permission" for RSV-2CE (it did not — the Scripture notice said "All rights reserved"; only the Catechism notice says "Used with Permission"), and treated the absence of permission documentation as a stop-ship, when under the gratis policy no such document exists to find.

**Additions grown from Patrick's review notes:** the "More Than Biology" why-questions paragraph rewritten as an argument (natural selection creates nothing, only selects); a problem-of-evil passage (naming evil — untrue, unjust, unmerciful, selfish, the four shadows of the pillars — presupposes an objective good; the atheist's protest is an ache for the good, "and that ache has an Author"); the TJMS convergence argument (four realities converging on one focal point is itself evidence of a single source) expanded into the "How We Know God Is Love" binds-paragraph; a counterexamples paragraph (the three practical scenes with love withheld; evil as Augustinian privation; "the counterfeit proves the currency," foreshadowing Ch. 15); the meaning of life stated plainly in "Against Meaninglessness" (receive, return, give away; Baltimore Catechism know/love/serve), ending "We were made by love, and we were made for love" — a verbatim plant of the epilogue's refrain.

**Epilogue edit (same session):** new promise-kept paragraph after the gratitude paragraph — John 16:13 quoted (RSV), "all the truth" not only what would be bound in a book, the Church led deeper into His love, CCC 25 cited as a six-word callback ("the love that never ends") rather than re-quoted since Ch. 2 opens with the full text and Ch. 17 pairs both clauses with Romans 12:21; the passing "whom the Holy Spirit has led into all truth" clause removed from the thirty-seven-years sentence so the promise fires once with full weight. Patrick's wider "lay down the gauntlet" idea was deliberately kept out of Ch. 3 (per the decision that the explicit magisterial argument lives in the epilogue only) and satisfied by this epilogue paragraph's confident-but-invitational form. ### 20. ✗ DECLINED Red-Letter Formatting for Jesus’ Words (2026-08-17)

Patrick’s underlying instinct was sound and worth naming: the Shema/Great Commandment already functions in this book as “the grand hermeneutical key” (see item 10) — the corrective to reading Paul’s faith language apart from what Jesus Himself taught, per Galatians 5:6’s “faith working through love” and Dei Verbum’s Christ-centered hermeneutic (DV 19–21; CCC 65). But red-letter typography was judged the wrong tool for it: it marks every line of Gospel dialogue identically, which flattens rather than highlights the specific hinge-passages (the Great Commandment) that actually carry the interpretive weight; it visually implies a two-tier inspiration that Dei Verbum 11 explicitly rules out (all Scripture, “with all its parts,” equally inspired — Paul included); and the term now carries baggage from the “Red Letter Christians” progressive-evangelical movement (Campolo/Claiborne, founded 2007), which uses exactly this device to argue Jesus’ words override the rest of the moral tradition. A narrower alternative (a distinct callout style reserved just for the Shema/Great Commandment citations) was proposed and also declined by Patrick.

**Decision: no red-letter formatting anywhere in the book, and no callout style either.** The hermeneutical-key argument stays carried entirely by the prose (item 10’s nine-chapter cross-reference thread), which already does the job.

Audited every Mercy mark against this test across the Ch. 13 virtue matrix (all ten Mercy-marked virtues: Charity, Prudence, Generosity, Patience, Kindness, Wisdom, Mercy, Meekness, Gentleness, Zeal) and the Ch. 14 vice matrix.

The three vices flagged for review — **Lust, Injustice, and Betrayal** — are correctly left blank: each is a justice/dignity or covenant-fidelity offense (what is owed), not a withholding of relief beyond what's owed. **Lukewarmness**, the one asymmetric case (privation of Zeal, which carries a Mercy star, yet itself carries none), is already explained in Ch. 14's own prose — it goes cold on truth while "the kindness continues," so Mercy genuinely isn't offended there.
